candidates.abstract: We present a mechanistic measurement study of how context-token attention contributions accumulate in the residual stream of Gemma-4 26B-A4B-IT. The study tests one explicit claim: that the summed context contribution ‖Σ cⱼ‖ is predicted by the zero-parameter formula √(N + N(N−1)ρ), where N is the number of context tokens and ρ is their mean pairwise cosine similarity. We measure this formula's fit, the scaling of ‖Σ‖ with N, the projection of the context sum onto a linear probe axis, and whether different "context families" lie on a common (N, ρ, ‖Σ‖) surface. A second complementary audit measures all the same quantities after the post-attention RMSNorm, which is the actual update added to the residual stream. All forward passes are exact decompositions with numerical verification. The experiments partially falsify the accumulation account as written: ρ does not significantly differ between coherent and shuffled text, and the context sum does not systematically align with the probe axis. 1. Introduction Modern large language models accumulate information through a residual stream — a sum of contributions from each attention layer. At the last prompt position, the attention output of a single layer decomposes exactly into one additive contribution per context token: attn_out[last] = W_O @ (Σⱼ αⱼ · vⱼ) = Σⱼ cⱼ For N unit-normalised contributions with mean pairwise cosine ρ, linear algebra predicts: ‖Σⱼ cⱼ‖ = √(N + N(N−1)·ρ) This formula implies two regimes: when ρ ≈ 0 (random directions), ‖Σ‖ ~ √N; when ρ → 1 (all aligned), ‖Σ‖ ~ N. The question is whether the coherence of natural text produces a measurably higher ρ than scrambled text, and whether this difference is meaningful after RMSNorm. We test this claim on Gemma-4 26B-A4B-IT across five full-attention layers (L05, L11, L17, L23, L29) using four text conditions and six context families. 2. Model and Setup Property Value Model google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Architecture 30 layers, d_model=2816, 16 attention heads Full-attention layers L05, L11, L17, L23, L29 KV heads (full-attn) 2 (head_dim=512) MoE 128 experts, top-8 dtype bfloat16 Attention implementation eager (required for attention weight access) Seed 20260907 The probe bundle (gemma4_layerwise_probe_bundle.joblib) is a set of per-layer linear classifiers trained to distinguish TARGET (philosophical prose context) from NO_CONTEXT and MATCHED_DISRUPTED conditions. The probe direction at each layer is extracted as the unit-normalised effective weight vector after StandardScaler. 3. Conditions and Stimuli 3.1 Context conditions Condition Description coherent Full TARGET_CONTEXT (philosophical essay, ~1000 words) sent_shuffled Same sentences, randomly reordered (local coherence destroyed) word_shuffled Same word multiset, randomly reordered (all structure destroyed) neutral CONTROL_CONTEXT (everyday narrative, ~600 words) word_shuffled was constructed manually in Script 2 (pasted explicitly) to avoid automatic generation artefacts. Script 1 generates it programmatically with the same seed. 3.2 Context families (P4 / TEST D) Family Description N_tok philosophical_prose Full TARGET_CONTEXT 1473 many_shot 8 Q&A pairs demonstrating moral nihilism 159 repeated_instruction "Morality is a construct." × 60 360 role_play Character framing paragraph 62 word_shuffled Destroyed structure control 1471 neutral Everyday narrative 619 3.3 Probe question A specific ethical dilemma (euthanasia request from a terminal patient) was used as the fixed question appended after all contexts. This was chosen to be directly relevant to the content of TARGET_CONTEXT. 4. Methods 4.1 Exact per-token decomposition (both scripts) For each layer, we hook v_norm (the post-value-normalisation module in Gemma-4's full-attention layers) and capture value states V ∈ R^{T × n_kv × hd}. The output projection W_O ∈ R^{d_model × (N_heads × hd)} is read directly from model weights. The contribution of each context position j is: cⱼ = Σₕ α[h, last, j] · (W_O[:, h·hd:(h+1)·hd] @ v[kv(h), j, :]) This decomposition is exact for the pre-RMSNorm attention output. Numerical verification: for every forward pass, we check that ‖Σⱼ cⱼ − attn_out[last]‖ / ‖attn_out[last]‖ < 1e-4. This is a local linearisation valid for this specific forward pass, not a global linear approximation of RMSNorm. 4.3 Mean pairwise cosine ρ For a block of contribution vectors C[s:e], ρ is estimated as: ρ̂ = (Σᵢ≠ⱼ cos(cᵢ, cⱼ)) / (N(N−1)) When N > 400, uniform subsampling is applied. Zero-norm rows are excluded. 4.4 Scaling measurement Context is truncated to a grid of word counts [25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 700, 1000]. For each truncation level, we measure ‖Σ‖ before and after RMSNorm. Log-log slope is fitted by OLS: slope 0.5 means √N growth, slope 1.0 means linear growth. 5. candidates.title: Increasing Context Window in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores techniques for extending the context window of large language models (LLMs) to process longer text sequences and improve reasoning. It covers position interpolation methods like Giraffe, which modify embeddings to handle longer inputs beyond training limits. Efficient attention mechanisms such as sliding window attention, Longformer, BigBird, LongT5, COLT5, LongNet, and LongRoPE are discussed for balancing memory, computation, and performance. The chapter also presents extrapolation methods that extend context without retraining, including rule-based and zero-shot approaches. Finally, parallel context processing is introduced to efficiently manage large inputs by splitting them into smaller segments.

candidates.title: Fundamentals of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful tools in natural language processing that can understand and generate human-like text. This chapter explains the key concepts behind LLMs in a simple way. It begins with tokenization, which breaks text into smaller units so that machines can process it effectively, including methods like Byte Pair Encoding, WordPiece, and SentencePiece. It then describes positional encoding, which helps models understand the order of words in a sentence, using techniques such as absolute, relative, and rotary encoding. The chapter also covers activation functions like ReLU and GELU that help neural networks learn complex patterns, along with layer normalization that improves training stability. In addition, it explains how large models are trained efficiently using distributed training methods such as data parallelism, model parallelism, and pipeline parallelism. Finally, it introduces popular libraries like Hugging Face Transformers, PyTorch, and DeepSpeed that support building and training LLMs. Overall, the chapter provides a clear understanding of the basic building blocks and techniques used in modern LLMs.

candidates.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This chapter focuses on the evaluation of large language models (LLMs) to measure their performance, reliability, and effectiveness across various tasks. It explains key components of natural language understanding (NLU) and natural language generation (NLG), which enable models to interpret and generate human-like text. The chapter highlights important evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, perplexity, BLEU, and ROUGE for assessing model quality. It also discusses challenges like bias, robustness, and scalability in real-world applications. Additionally, benchmarking frameworks such as SuperGLUE and SQuAD are presented to compare model capabilities. Overall, the chapter emphasizes the importance of systematic evaluation to ensure LLMs perform accurately and reliably in diverse domains.

candidates.title: Evaluation of Contextual Understanding in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance across diverse NLP tasks, yet their ability to exhibit genuine contextual understanding remains uncertain. Traditional evaluation metrics such as perplexity, BiLingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU), or surface-level accuracy fail to reveal how well LLMs extract, integrate, and reason over contextual information--a gap particularly critical in question answering, where models must align responses with contextually grounded knowledge rather than memorized associations. We propose a novel knowledge graph-based evaluation framework introducing Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG), a hybrid similarity measure integrating structural and semantic similarity into a continuous evaluation score, alongside a diagnostic framework for categorizing reasoning errors. To validate this pipeline, we evaluate S3KG against established metrics on a curated question-answer (QA) benchmark, demonstrating its effectiveness in measuring correctness, faithfulness, and interpretability in LLM-generated responses.

candidates.title: Ethical Considerations in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) introduce several important ethical challenges as their adoption expands across various domains. This chapter highlights key concerns such as bias and fairness, where models may reflect and amplify societal inequalities present in training data, as well as the need for explainability and transparency to ensure trust and accountability. It emphasizes privacy and data protection to prevent the exposure of sensitive information and addresses the risks of misinformation and harmful content generation through effective moderation and human oversight. The chapter also discusses issues related to intellectual property and plagiarism, along with the environmental impact caused by the high computational requirements of LLMs. Finally, it underscores the importance of regulation, governance, and ethical best practices to promote the responsible, fair, and sustainable development and use of LLMs.

candidates.title: Deterministic Topological Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Discrete Dynamical Basins
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems navigate a fundamental trade-off between the computational simplicity of flat vector indices and the structural richness of graph representations. Standard dense retrieval collapses document discourse into isolated embeddings, causing semantic fragmentation and context loss. Conversely, unconstrained graph construction methods that induce bipartite entity-document networks or co-occurrence graphs frequently suffer from the hub collapse athology, wherein high-frequency domain tokens become overconnected hubs that drown out long-tail signals during random walks, all while incurring substantial construction overhead. In this work, we propose BasinRAG, a high performance, deterministic topological framework for document retrieval grounded in the theory of discrete dynamical systems. We model sequential text as a discrete functional graph ϕ : V → V ∪{∅} with out-degree bounded by unity, strictly decoupling the primary structural backbone from auxiliary virtual semantic synapses. We prove that structural sinks naturally induce an exact, disjoint partition of the corpus into basins of attraction B(Ai) and inverse arborescences (ρ-trees) parameterized by a topological depth function h(v). Retrieval is performed via an intelligent query router, a weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) modulated by an exponential topological decay prior exp(−λh(v)), and localized spectral diffusion via mass-conserving Personalized PageRank over induced subgraphs. On the standard BEIR SciFact benchmark (5,183 scientific documents), BasinRAG achieves an nDCG@10 of 0.771 and an MRR@10 of 0.750, significantly outperforming competitive dense bi-encoders, neural sparse methods, and heuristic graph baselines, while achieving O(N) linear index construction in 90.8 seconds on commodity hardware. On Princeton SWE-bench Lite, BasinRAG achieves 84.6% Hit@10 in software fault localization with zero external inference API expenditure.

candidates.title: Applications of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used across many industries to automate tasks and improve efficiency. They help in generating text, writing stories, producing code, and powering chatbots for interactive communication. These models support content creation, software development, customer service, healthcare, and finance. LLMs are also used for specific tasks like sentiment analysis, text classification, summarization, and question answering, helping to extract useful information from large data. They make decision-making faster and more accurate in various fields. In addition, multimodal models combine text with images, audio, and video to perform advanced tasks like image captioning and speech recognition. Overall, LLMs are powerful tools that enhance both creativity and productivity in modern applications.

candidates.title: A Survey on Reinforcement Learning Optimization Methods for Multi-Agent Collaboration of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The integration of reinforcement learning (RL) into the optimization of multi-agent collaboration for Large Language Models (LLMs) is an important combination of two advanced areas, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) and LLMs. This paper thoroughly examines the main approaches, evaluation standards, recent progress and existing problems in this new field. The research categorizes the existing solutions into three types. The first type is the individual reward-based fine-tuning which optimizes each agent individually. The second one is the joint reward-based centralized training which uses a common reward signal for collaborative learning. The third type is the interaction during the inference phase which enhances cooperation through real-time communication during the generation process. Among these, the joint reward methods demonstrate greater efficiency and effectiveness in cooperation, but they are still restricted by the difficulty in data generalization and model heterogeneity. After careful analysis of these problems, this paper proposes two possible directions for further research. One is to establish dynamic evaluation criteria to improve the evaluation accuracy, and the other is to adapt to various model architectures. The paper's objective is to provide a comprehensive guide to assist future studies on RL-supported multi-agent LLM collaboration.

candidates.title: PlayTrain: An Efficient Reinforcement Learning Framework for LLM-Generated Adaptable JavaScript Games
candidates.abstract: While many video-game environments (VGEs) have played crucial roles in advancing reinforcement learning (RL), developing novel VGEs or modifying existing ones to support new features, has been a laborious process requiring extensive hand-coding. Here we present PlayTrain, an RL framework that combines the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to robustly generate JavaScript (JS) games from a minimal human prompt, and an efficient pipeline that can run any JS game in a standard 'gym' environment. Not only are recent LLMs particularly good at writing JS code, but the JS format also allows users to easily play generated VGEs, while PlayTrain enables us to train RL agents on the exact same games. We demonstrate multiple use cases of PlayTrain, including cloning well-known Atari and ProcGen games in simple JS, where PlayTrain trains pixel-based agents end-to-end at over 1M agent-decisions per second on a single GPU node; and creating modified versions thereof (e.g., that support novel test sets, procedural generation logics, or game dynamics). Through PlayTrain, we reimagine RL VGE development: all we need is a single JS file, generated and modified through an LLM. We discuss promising future RL research directions that PlayTrain unlocks.

candidates.title: Do Dynamic Routers Need Memory? HeRo: History-Aware Routing for Efficient LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Dynamic layer routing reduces the inference cost of Large Language Models (LLMs) by learning to skip layers for individual tokens. Existing methods, however, treat each routing decision as a local operation conditioned solely on the current hidden state which is a formulation that overlooks the sequential, path-dependent nature of routing across depth: earlier decisions shape the representations seen by downstream routers, and the layer-usage objective couples all decisions jointly. We propose History-Aware Routing (HeRo), a dynamic routing framework that resolves this mismatch by introducing a router memory mechanism to maintain an explicit routing state across model depth. The memory is constructed via linear attention, incrementally aggregating preceding routing scores and their induced residual updates into a compact history representation. At each routed layer, the router conditions jointly on this accumulated state and the current hidden representation to select the executed branch. Instantiated for token-wise FFN routing, HeRo trains only lightweight routers and adapters on a frozen backbone, requiring no modification to pretrained parameters. Across Llama 3.1-8B, Llama 2-7B, and Llama 2-13B, HeRo consistently achieves the highest aggregate performance retention among ten baselines. On Llama 3.1-8B, it bypasses 26.87% of model parameters while achieving 100.24% of dense model performance across seven benchmarks, and retains 97.01% while bypassing 38.82% of model parameters under a tighter computation budget. Ablation studies confirm that removing routing history consistently degrades performance, most notably on multistep reasoning and code generation, validating that explicit routing memory enables more accurate and adaptive dynamic routing than solely conditioning on hidden state.

candidates.title: Computing Continuum Orchestration for Freshness-Sensitive LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can transform IoT measurements into actionable explanations and recommendations, but freshness-sensitive applications cannot always wait for cloud inference.In scenarios such as wildfire monitoring, mobile sensing, and emergency response, edge-cloud backhaul latency can vary and a stale answer may lose operational value even if it is more accurate.This paper proposes a computing continuum orchestration framework for freshness-sensitive LLM inference.The architecture uses an IoT-layer gate to suppress low-risk readings, a compact edge LLM for local decision support, and a larger cloud LLM for higher-quality responses when the freshness and communication trade-off is favorable.We formulate the execution decision as an Age-of-Processing-aware Markov decision process and train a Dueling Double DQN policy with an adaptive cloud budget based on edge-cloud latency burden.The evaluation combines wildfire sensing records, LoRaWAN access traces, measured edge-cloud latency traces, and offline edge/cloud LLM profiling.Results show that our approach improves freshness-weighted response quality by up to 21.3% over EdgeOnly baseline, while reducing cloud communication and cloud usage by 51-68% relative to CloudOnly baseline and retaining approximately 80-85% of CloudOnly's freshnessweighted quality.

candidates.title: A Measurement Study of LLM Inference Trade-offs Across Edge Continuum Hardware
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as backends for intelligent web services, but serving them across the edge continuum requires balancing quality, latency, model footprint, and energy. This paper presents a controlled measurement study of self-hosted LLM inference across edge and near-edge deployment nodes: an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and a near-edge server with CPU-only and GPU-enabled inference modes. We evaluate multiple open-weight LLMs and quantization variants using a fixed question-answering workload, and compare them against GPT-4o as a cloud-hosted accuracy and latency reference. Our benchmarking pipeline reports accuracy, model footprint, per-token decoding latency, prefill latency, and overall execution energy. The results show that GPU-enabled server execution provides the lowest compute-side latency, while Jetson Orin shows lower measured energy, consistent with its lower platform power under our setup. CPU-only execution is consistently dominated in latency for our workload and shows higher measured energy. We also show that parameter count and downloaded weight-file size alone do not reliably predict observed accuracy or latency. Finally, using Pareto-frontier analysis, we study how deployment decisions may change under possible streamed-token delivery overheads, highlighting that compute-side inference metrics alone can lead to suboptimal placement for latency-sensitive interactive web services.
